new_statements.quote: Acento. Em concani, a última sílaba ou vogal duma palavra é sempre acentuada e, portanto, longa, a não ser que seja a vogal ò muda, porque nesse caso o acento recai na penúltima. Exemplos: ambó (manga); koli (cadela); vòstú (coisas); pollé (olha tu); marít (batendo); roddót (chorando). Nos ditongos finais é acentuada a primeira vogal quando a segunda seja i ou u. Ex.: xapái (avô); kolói (estanho); bapúi (pai). Aliás, leva o acento a segunda vogal — Ex.: doriá (mar); boriák (para o bem); diúnk (para dar); gôriô (anzóis).
new_statements.translation: Accent. In Konkani the last syllable or vowel of a word is always accented and therefore long, unless it is the mute vowel ò, in which case the accent falls on the penultimate. Examples: ambó 'mango', koli 'bitch', vòstú 'things', pollé 'look!', marít 'beating', roddót 'crying'. In final diphthongs the first vowel is accented when the second is i or u, e.g. xapái 'grandfather', kolói 'tin', bapúi 'father'. Otherwise the second vowel carries the accent, e.g. doriá 'sea', boriák 'for the good', diúnk 'to give', gôriô 'fish-hooks'.
new_statements.citation: Morais, Graciano. 1950. Transliteração da língua concani em caracteres romanos. (Publicações do Instituto de Línguas Africanas e Orientais, anexo à Escola Superior Colonial, I; extr. de Estudos Coloniais II, 1950-51.) Lisboa. Section 'Acento', pp. 27-28.
new_statements.locator: pp. 27-28, heading 'Acento' (PDF leaf 14 right half and leaf 15 left half; djvu the text layer)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: has no text layer; I rendered PDF leaves 14-15 (2-up scan) and read the page image. p. 27 heading 'Acento': "Em concani, a última sílaba ou vogal duma palavra é sempre acentuada e, portanto, longa, a não ser que seja a vogal ò muda, porque nesse caso o acento recai na penúltima. Exemplos: ambó (manga); koli (cadela); vòstú (coisas); pollé (olha tu); marít (batendo); roddót (chorando)." p. 28: "Nos ditongos finais é acentuada a primeira vogal quando a segunda seja i ou u. Ex.: xapái (avô); kolói (estanho); bapúi (pai). Aliás, leva o acento a segunda vogal — Ex.: doriá (mar); boriák (para o bem); diúnk (para dar); gôriô (anzóis)." Verbatim as reported (only trivial diacritic rend…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent falls on the final syllable (the final full vowel, which is thereby long); a word whose last vowel is the reduced 'mute ò' (reflex of final short a) is stressed on the penult, i.e. on the last full syllable. In word-final vowel sequences Vi/Vu the first vowel is stressed, in other sequences (iá, iú, ió) the second. Dalgado 1905 p. XXXII states the same distribution in quantity terms: words ending in a long vowel are oxytone, words ending in mute a or another short vowel are paroxytone, exceptions only in unassimilated foreign words; LSI VII p.167 concurs ('accent usually rests on the final syllable, though never on the short vowel pronounced after a final consonant').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in Morais 1950 or Dalgado 1905.
new_statements.exceptions: Morais: final mute ò -> penult stress; final diphthongs in -i/-u stress the first vowel. Dalgado 1905 rule 22: words ending in mute a or other short vowel are paroxytone; 'As excepções limitam-se a vocabulos exoticos não popularizados' (unassimilated loans); rule 23: in song/poetry final a is replaced by short i/u without shifting the accent. Morais 1961 §422-423: accent moves to a suffixal final vowel (hòsó; Devóch).
new_statements.domain_note: Stated for the word ('duma palavra') on citation forms; an orthographic/pronunciation treatise, impressionistic, equating accent with vowel length. Dalgado's formulation is quantity-based (final long vowel vs final short/mute vowel), so a 'weight-sensitive, right-edge two-syllable window' reading is also defensible; Bhat & Bai 2004 note for (Kerala) Konkani that stress is non-contrastive and perceived as length, and a modern second-hand source (Menezes via Wikipedia) says Konkani has no phonemic stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Morais 1950 and Dalgado 1905 both describe the Konkani of Goa (Morais: Romi-script Goan Konkani, author a Goan priest and 'leitor de concanim' in Lisbon; Dalgado: native of Bardez, Goa, dictionary of Goan Konkani) = goan1235. The catalog's existing Konkani entry (konk1267) rests on Maffei 1882, which is Mangalore/Canara Christian Konkani; Bhat & Bai 2004 (also final stress) is Kochi GSB Konkani; LSI 1905 and Katre 1966 are pan-dialectal. Dhongde 2022 (list of works to obtain) is explicitly the Goan (Panaji) standard.

new_statements.quote: § 44. STRESS. Stress is denoted by [ˈ] before the syllable which bears it. Word stress is generally initial, but may be varied according to the needs of the speaker in order to emphasize a particular shade of meaning ; an example of this has been already given in §40. Since there is no well-defined word order in Konkani, word-stress is subordinate to sentence-stress, and this will depend upon the sense in which they are used. In words borrowed from Sanscrit, stress is generally on the heaviest syllable ; and as a result of this tendency proper names are stressed similarly. [...] Unlike in Bengali all words, including pronominals, conjunctions and other particles are stressed.
new_statements.citation: Katre, S. M. 1935. Konkani Phonetics. Journal of the Department of Letters (University of Calcutta) 27: 1-19 [article pagination]. Sec. 44 'Stress', p. 17.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 44 STRESS, p. 17 of the article (page header 'KONKANI PHONETICS 17' immediately precedes it); dialect basis sec. 3, p. 3
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: lines 17409-17440, under the page header 'KO[N]KA[N]I PHONETICS 17' (line 17397): '§ 44. STRESS. Stress is denoted by [*^] before the syllable which bears it. Word stress is generally initial, but may be varied according to the needs of the speaker in order to emphasize a particular shade of meaning; an example of this has been already given in §40. Since the^e is no well-defined word order in Konkani, word-stress is subordinate to sentence-stress.. In words borrowed from Sanscrit, stress is generally on the heaviest syllable; and as a result of this tendency proper names are stressed similarly.. Unlike in Bengali all words, including pronominals, conjunctions and other particles are stress…
new_statements.relation_note: The existing statement (Morais 1950, pp. 27-28, Goan Christian orthography) puts the accent on the last pronounced syllable; Grierson 1905 p. 167 and Dalgado 1905 p. XXXII (in from our earlier reading) also say final. Katre 1935 says word stress is 'generally initial'. The difference is partly one of variety: Katre states in sec. 3 'My own dialect is sK. [Konkani of the Kanara Saraswat Brahmins] belonging to the central group.. the field has been restricted principally to the central groups', whereas Morais and Dalgado describe the Goan (Christian, Portuguese-orthography) speech. Katre's own sec. 40 example [bo'do:] 'very' shows non-initial stress even in sK.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable as the default, but it is weak: it yields to sentence stress and can be shifted for emphasis; Sanskrit loanwords and proper names take stress on the heaviest syllable. Sec. 40 (p. 15) shows the stress deciding which schwa is lengthened in disyllables: ['dzordo] 'heavy' vs [bo'do:] 'very', i.e. some native words carry final stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 17: 'For the purpose of stress K. words have to be divided into several syllabic groups, since a secondary stress is developed in polysyllabic groups; generally two syllables form one group, except when the next contains the neutral vowel, in which case it may also be included in this group.' Marked with a grave accent, e.g. ['modhuˌkoru] Madhukaru; in a sense-group the secondary stress 'is likely to be slurred over'.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress may be varied by the speaker for emphasis; word stress is subordinate to sentence stress; Sanskrit borrowings and proper names are stressed on the heaviest syllable; monosyllables always have a long vowel and vocatives a long final vowel (sec. 43, p. 17); intonation 'is not very significant' (sec. 45).
new_statements.identity_note: Katre 1935 covers all Konkani dialects under one label (Ratnagiri north to Cochin) but the phonetic description is explicitly of sK., the Konkani of the Kanara Saraswat Brahmins (central group), with gsK. (Gauda Saraswat), xK. (Christians of Goa and the Kanaras), nK. (Ratnagiri) and cK. (Cochin) cited only in comparison. Kanara Saraswat Konkani is generally subsumed under ISO gom / goan1235, but it is not the Goan Christian variety that Morais 1950 and Dalgado 1905 describe. Vaz 2018 (not opened) is about the Salcete Christian dialect of Goa (Sudir Gawdas).

readall_conflicts: The sources disagree on placement. Morais 1950 (pp. 27-28; the existing statement), Dalgado 1905 (p. XXXII, rule 22) and Grierson 1905 (LSI VII p. 167) put the accent on the final (last pronounced) syllable of Goan Konkani, all three describing the Goan Christian / Portuguese-orthography speech. Katre 1935 (sec. 44, p. 17) says 'Word stress is generally initial', subordinate to sentence stress and shifted to the heaviest syllable in Sanskrit loans, and his description rests on his own Kanara Saraswat dialect (sK., sec. 3), with the Goan Christian dialect (xK.) only compared; Katre 1966 sec. 25 (earlier check) repeats 'initial' in a historical-phonology sense. Bhat & Bai 2004 (Kochi GSB Konkani, not Goan) give final stress. So the split is initial (Katre, Saraswat basis) versus final (Morais, Dalgado, Grierson, Goan Christian basis; Bhat & Bai for Kochi), and the Wikipedia sentence attributed to the unreachable Menezes poster claims Konkani has no phonemic stress at all. Whether the disagreement is dialectal, or a difference between phonetic prominence and orthographic accent-length marking, cannot be settled from the works opened.
